title: Knowing how to die
hookLine: Guru Nanak: death wouldn't be called bad if people knew how truly to die

cards: A family is mourning. Someone says what people say: what a terrible thing, death. And a hymn in the Guru Granth Sahib, the Sikh scripture, answers back, gently.
On page 579, in verses Guru Nanak gave for times of mourning, comes a line that, put plainly, runs like this: people, don't call death bad, if only someone knew how truly to die.
The hymn doesn't argue that death is pleasant. It moves the problem. The trouble isn't dying.

teach.b: Death sounds like something that simply happens to you. Nobody takes a class in it. But the hymn speaks of it as a skill, something a person can know or not know.
Where is it learned? In Sikh teaching, as the Gurus describe it, a person who lives remembering the divine Name, serving others and living honestly is already practicing for the end.
The same verses speak of serving the Lord and of the true court a person goes to after this life. So knowing how to die isn't a last-minute trick. It's what a whole life has been rehearsing.
Sikhs have a phrase for this: dying while alive. Some Sikh readers hear it as letting the ego die now, the grasping, the need to win, so that when death comes there's less left to tear away.
Readers explain it in different ways, but the shape is simple: practice letting go in small things, and the big letting go is less of a stranger. The hymn was given for mourning.
But if a whole life is the rehearsal, then the rehearsal is happening this afternoon, in an hour spent scrolling or an hour spent with someone you love.
Read that way, the question shifts from how long a life runs to how the hour in front of you is lived.

how: Sikhs hear the Gurus' hymns on death in the gurdwara and at funerals, where the evening hymns of Kirtan Sohila are sung; Sikh teaching describes remembering the Name, honest work and service as the way a life prepares for its end.

o: a word for the grief mourners feel after someone dies
a Sikh funeral rite where the body is carried to the fire
death, in Guru Nanak's hymn: not bad, if one knows how to die

games.q: the pieces of the hymn — tap the pairs.
p: learned by the way you live

s: the hymn says death is pleasant and nothing to grieve
it doesn't call death pleasant. it moves the trouble to not knowing how to die.
the verses come from a set Guru Nanak gave for times of mourning
they sit on page 579 of the Guru Granth Sahib.
in Sikh teaching, knowing how to die is a trick learned at the very end

games.q: you're at a family's side after a death. someone says, death is a terrible thing. the hymn speaks. what does it say?
o: death is a punishment, so be afraid of it.
don't call death bad, if one knew how truly to die.
don't think about death at all.
games.why: Guru Nanak's line doesn't deny the grief. it moves the question: the trouble isn't death, it's not knowing how to die.

practice: Look at the next hour of your day, just the next hour: where you'll be, and who will be there.
Ask it one quiet question, if this hour were lived well, what would it look like, slower, kinder, one thing done properly instead of three done badly, and let one small picture come.
If you pray, you can hold that hour up in your own tradition's words.

wordCard.voice: Maran, the Gurmukhi word for death in Guru Nanak's hymn, which says the trouble isn't dying, but not knowing how, learned by living. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi, the script of the Guru Granth Sahib: maran, death, from the line on page 579.

carryVoice: Your line: knowing how. A whole life is the rehearsal. That's day seven hundred eighty-seven.
